books.section: Topic 6.9 Responses to Immigration in the Gilded Age

primary_sources: Henry Cabot Lodge, “The Restriction of Immigration,” North American Review, January 1891

stimulus.text:
“Thus it is proved, first, that immigration to this country is increasing, and, second, that it is making its greatest relative increase from races most alien to the body of the American people and from the lowest and most illiterate classes among those races. In other words, it is apparent that, while our immigration is increasing, it is showing at the same time a marked tendency to deteriorate in character.”

Henry Cabot Lodge, “The Restriction of Immigration,” North American Review, January 1891.
stimulus.source_note: Henry Cabot Lodge, “The Restriction of Immigration,” North American Review, vol. 152 (January 1891), p. 32, as reprinted in Publications of the Immigration Restriction League, No. 1 (1894). Public domain; text checked against the Internet Archive scan of the League’s Publications.

stem: Lodge called the new immigrants “the lowest and most illiterate classes among those races.” That language best reflects which broader Gilded Age idea?

options.text: The settlement house belief that all classes depend on each other
options.misconception: Names the settlement belief, which welcomed immigrants instead.

options.text: The Populist demand for the free coinage of silver
options.misconception: Names a money policy with nothing to do with immigrants.

options.text: The nativist fear that new immigrants would weaken American identity
The Gospel of Wealth idea that the rich should fund libraries
options.misconception: Names Carnegie's giving, which has nothing to do with immigrants.

rationales.A: Settlement workers believed classes depend on each other and aided immigrants. Lodge's words attack the newcomers, not aid them.
rationales.B: Free silver was a Populist money demand. It says nothing about immigrants or American identity.
rationales.C: Lodge judges the new immigrants by race and literacy and warns that immigration is deteriorating in character. That is the nativist fear: that newcomers unlike earlier Americans would weaken what America was.
rationales.D: Carnegie's gospel told the rich to fund libraries. It says nothing about judging immigrants by race.
rationales.general:
Ask what fear the insult is serving.
1. Lodge sorts immigrants by race and calls the new ones the lowest and most illiterate classes.
2. He warns that immigration is deteriorating in character.
3. Background from the books: nativists feared new immigrants would weaken American identity.
4. So the language is nativist fear, not settlement aid, silver money, or rich men's giving.
Remember: an insult that sorts people by race is serving a fear about who belongs.
